summary: Wilde's letter to his sister-in-law Nellie Lloyd on the birth of his first son, written the same day as the telegram to her husband.
certainty_reasoning: The record documents a friendship or acquaintance with no evidence of attraction or romance; classified platonic, upgradable if contrary evidence comes to light.

sources.quote:
My dear Little Nellie, You will be delighted to hear that Constance got through her confinement all right, suffering hardly any pain. The child - an amazing boy! - was born when she was under chloroform, and on coming to she absolutely declined to believe it was born at all! And was only convinced of the fact by the nurse producing a stalward boy, _who already knows me quite well_. She is very happy and peaceful but cannot see anyone for some days. The doctor has posted a bulletin in the hall to that effect.

You must have a little girl and we will make up a match at once. I will let you and Otho, the important uncle and aunt of our son and heir, know how she gets on. I hope you will get through your own confinement as easily as Constance - I am sure you will. It really is very little after all - you must not be nervous. I have sent Otho a telegram and send you a letter (my first!). I know you will be delighted – both of you. Ever affectionately yours

OSCAR
sources.context: Wilde to Nellie Lloyd, [postmark 5 June 1885], 16 Tite Street (MS Holland), written the same day as the telegram to her husband. The letter breaks where the printed page does. 'who already knows me quite well' is underlined in the original. Wilde was thirty and had been married eleven months.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde on the birth of his first son, to his sister-in-law, the same morning.
